audit: The glovebox analogy explains containment but can obscure the fact that the harness should retain credentials while the program receives only projected data. Lesson A supplies literal input files, sandbox limits and release criteria in separately owned containers. The learner identifies why a safe chart workflow does not need a production token inside generated code. Lesson B compares two output collectors under a constructed hostile stream: one stops capture at its configured cap, while the other exceeds its available buffer before final truncation. This isolates an enforcement-timing defect without inventing a benchmark or claiming any sandbox technology is universally stronger than another.

lessons.title: Pass the CSV through the glovebox opening
lessons.intro: An authorized analyst requests a sales chart for store S-7. The harness obtains only the required rows and exposes them to a disposable execution environment.

relations: Harness passes scoped data, not its credential.
Only inspected, authorized artifacts may leave.

read: Locate the credential outside the execution chamber.
The generated program receives the authorized data slice only.
The output gate checks content and entitlement before release.
lessons.question: Does a chart.png filename alone satisfy the release gate?
lessons.answer: No. The gate must parse the actual type, enforce size limits and verify that the content is appropriate for the requester. An extension does not establish safe format or authorized disclosure.
lessons.takeaway: Contain input authority and inspect output release separately.
lessons.assumption: Fictional limits; the runtime enforces them externally. Destruction removes the execution copy under its contract, not every retained artifact.

lessons.anchor: Build it: an isolated Python execution tool
lessons.title: A limit must act before the collector fills
lessons.intro: A hostile program attempts to emit 10 MiB. Both designs promise a 64 KiB returned transcript. The collector can hold only 1 MiB; compare when each cap is enforced.

data.input: 10 MiB stream; 64 KiB return cap; 1 MiB collector limit.

left.title: Cap during capture
steps: Count bytes as each stream chunk arrives
At 64 KiB, stop capture and signal limit
left.result: Captured output stays within 64 KiB; report output limit

right.title: Truncate after capture
steps: Append all emitted bytes to the collector
Cross 1 MiB before the program completes
Final truncation never protects the buffer
right.result: Collector limit is exceeded before any final 64 KiB slice

read: Both designs advertise the same final transcript size.
Only the left design enforces the bound while bytes arrive.
Artifact and scratch quotas remain separate from the stdout limit.
lessons.question: Would increasing the final truncation strictness to 32 KiB repair the right path?
lessons.answer: No. The failure occurs while accumulating bytes, before truncation. Enforce a streaming cap and bounded cleanup; separately constrain memory, artifacts, scratch storage and child processes.
lessons.takeaway: Enforce resource bounds during consumption, not after it.
lessons.assumption: Constructed sizes, not measured performance. The left provider enforces chunk accounting and termination; this example isolates output collection.
